transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what brings you here today?

I suppose what brings me in is… I just haven’t been myself since my friend was killed. Everyone kept saying time would help, and I know people mean well when they say things like that—my sister says it constantly, actually, she’s always been the practical one—but it hasn’t really eased.

I feel like I’m carrying this constant mix of guilt and fear and anger all the time. It’s just there, even when I’m doing ordinary things, like making tea or trying to read. I don’t know, I guess I’m tired of pretending it’s getting better when it isn’t.
Do you find yourself having upsetting thoughts or memories about your friend’s death that come up even when you don’t want them to?

Yes… yes, I do. It can come out of nowhere. Like if I’m waiting at a crosswalk and the signal changes, or I hear a truck coming up the street—that low growl of the engine—it’s like my mind just drops me right back there.

Even something silly, like one of those walking-tour maps, you know, the kind they hand out downtown with the little arrows and landmarks… my friend always liked those, actually, she’d insist on reading them even when I had a perfectly good sense of direction. But then I’ll see one and suddenly I can see her stepping off the curb again, so clearly, before I can stop it. It’s very sharp, like it’s happening right in front of me.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain places, people, or activities because they remind you of your friend or what happened?

Yes… I do. I go out of my way not to pass that intersection. I’ll take a ridiculous route around it, even if it adds time. There’s a little bakery on the next block I used to like—well, their almond croissants were never as good as the ones my husband used to bring home from that place near the university—but I don’t go there now because it’s too close.

And I’ve stopped signing up for most of the walking tours and those safety meetings they have in the neighborhood. I used to go, partly just to get out of the house, but the conversations always seem to circle back to what happened there, and I just… I can’t bear sitting through that.

Have you noticed that your thoughts about yourself or the world have become more negative since your friend’s death—like feeling guilty, blaming yourself, or thinking that the world is dangerous or unfair?

Yes… I think so. I keep going over it in my head, telling myself that if I’d chosen a different route that day, or if I’d made more of a fuss about that crossing before—because people had complained, you know, not just me, there was a whole thing at one of those town meetings, though half the time they spend more time discussing flower planters than actual safety—then maybe she’d still be here.

And then I get angry all over again. At myself, at the driver, at the town for letting that crossing stay the way it was. It just feels like… how can the world be that careless? One minute you’re walking with someone, and the next—well. I can’t stop thinking it should have been prevented.
Have you noticed that your mood has stayed consistently negative since your friend’s death—like feeling angry, guilty, or sad most of the time, even when you’re not thinking about what happened?

Yes… it has. It’s not just when I’m thinking directly about the accident, though of course that’s there. It’s like I’ve been carrying around this constant mix of guilt and fear and anger since she was killed.

People kept saying it would ease with time, and I suppose they meant well—people always say those things, like when my neighbor lost her sister and everyone brought casseroles for two weeks and then just stopped asking—but it hasn’t really lifted for me. I still feel sad or on edge or angry most of the time, even on days when nothing particular has happened.
